title: The Methylome, Aging and Disease, and the Potential Roles of Deuterium and 5-Formylcytosine
content: The methylation pathway is a major player in epigenetics, with sophisticated regulatory control dictating which genes are expressed through a complex mechanism of hypo- and hypermethylation of cytosine bases in DNA. In this paper, we show that 5-formylcytosine (5fC), a rare and poorly understood modified base, has powerful capabilities to influence DNA mutations and repair and alter the structure of nucloeosomes, as well as introducing DNA-protein cross-links. Ten-eleven translocation (TET) enzymes are responsible for removing methyl groups from cytosine bases, through sequential oxidation steps, and we argue that 5fC (an intermediary in TET enzyme modifications) is highly enriched in deuterium due to the high deuterium kinetic isotope effect (KIE) of TET enzymes. The presence of a deuteron impedes the step that converts 5fC to 5-carboxylcytosine (5caC). Furthermore, we suggest that, similar to trimethylamine oxide (TMAO), 5fC serves as a marker for deuterium overload in the one-carbon (1C) units carried by methionine in the methylation pathway and through methyl tetrahydrofolate (CH3-THF) and its derivatives. The gut microbiome is responsible for stripping deuterium out of carriers of 1C units, via hydrogen gas recycling. Nutrients such as choline, L-carnitine, and betaine supply 1C units bound to nitrogen atoms which feed into the 1C pool via microbial enzymes. The anaerobic archaea play an essential role, and, when they are under-represented, deuterium becomes enriched in the 1C units. This ultimately increases the number of 5fC bases in the DNA, leading to an accelerated rate of aging, associated with increased risk to infection, autoimmune disease, cardiovascular disease, and cancer. Oxidative stress due to deuterium overload in the ATPase nanomotors leads to suppression of TET enzyme activity, which induces hypermethylation of promoters of tumor suppressive enzymes, facilitating cancer progression. In this paper, we present a perspective for a new pathogenesis avenue due to a dysregulated methylome.
